#9784. Why does my challah have stretch marks?: How to stop your challah from tearing.

Recently, our Community Development Coordinator Kat Mayerovitch shared a very important update from the King Arthur Baking subreddit: a surprising amount of people were wondering why their challah has “stretch marks.”

If you’re not one of those people and don’t know exactly what that means, you may still be familiar with the problem: Sometimes, challah loaves come out of the oven with stretches or tears along the braided strands. It doesn’t affect the quality of the bread, but it does affect the appearance.

To address this issue, I asked our Baking School Curriculum Developer Jack Tissiere for their thoughts on this problem, and they identified two potential causes.

Challah dough rises twice: Once after it’s mixed (known as bulk fermentation) and a second time after the loaf is shaped or braided. Cutting short that second rise can lead to a challah that develops tears as it bakes. As Jack explains, “When we underproof our challah loaves (in other words, don't give them enough time to rise), the bread is still super active and energetic. When it hits the heat of the oven it expands energetically, and that sudden burst of volume before the dough sets can cause the bread to stretch or rip.”

How to fix: Give your braided challah loaf a little more time to rise before baking. Push the proof until the loaf is puffy and marshmallow-y; when you press it with a floured finger, the indent should slowly fill in, which is a sign that it’s ready to be baked. Sometimes, depending on the temperature of both your dough and your environment, this can take longer than the recipe says; trust your instincts rather than relying on the clock. If you fully proof the bread, when you put the loaf into the oven it’s less energetic, which means there isn’t as much oven spring (and subsequent tearing) while baking.

The other reason your challah may have stretch marks is because the loaves are shaped or braided too tightly. As Jack explains “When loaves are braided very tightly, they don’t have a lot of room to grow during the rising and baking process, causing stretches or tears as they expand.”

How to fix: Give your challah dough some slack when shaping: Braid loosely, allowing extra space for the dough to expand as it undergoes its final proof before baking. And for a pretty, even braid, start braiding from the middle; this video shows you how.

Ready to tackle your next braided loaf? Check out our Braided Challah recipe from The Big Book of Bread.

#9781. When is a coding agent's task actually done?

An agent stops typing and the spinner goes away. Is the task finished?

It's tempting to say yes. It isn't: the agent has only run out of things to do and is waiting for my next message. I haven't read the diff, the checks haven't run on the merged result, and nothing is on main.

So I treat 'done' as something I decide, not something the agent signals. When I'm happy with the changes, I mark the task done, and that's the point where it becomes ready to merge. Until then, an agent that went quiet is just a quiet agent.

The other side has a cost. If nothing ever closes a task for you, the 'waiting' ones pile up and you forget what's in them. In the tool I build, Styx, finished tasks archive themselves after seven days, which keeps the list from growing without end.

So what's your rule? Do you call it done when the agent stops, when the tests pass, when you've read the diff, or something else?

#9778. The Undo Button for Agents That Is Not a Fork

Posted on Nov 4 • Originally published at Medium

An agent renamed two methods, updated two files, and missed the third. The test suite went from green to two failures in one commit. Getting back to working code took one push and 1028 milliseconds, and it did not involve a sandbox at all.

Sponsored by Tensorlake. All experiments, numbers, and terminal output in this piece are my own, run live on their infrastructure.

Bad file edits are not the interesting failure. A single wrong line gets caught by the next test run and fixed in place.

The expensive failure is the coherent-looking refactor that is wrong across files. I gave an agent a normal task: rename the verbose DocumentStore methods and make build_index take a mapping instead of a list of pairs.

It did exactly that, in store.py and indexer.py. It did not touch api.py, which still passes a list.

Two of four files changed. Every changed file is internally consistent. The break lives in the one file the agent did not open, which is exactly the case code review is worst at catching and exactly what you get when an agent works from a partial view of the repository.

You cannot prompt your way out of this reliably. What you need is a cheap, exact way back.

I pushed the working tree, let the agent push its refactor, then pushed the original tree back.

Look at the tree hashes rather than the commits. d5aa2a70cae2e48f507367d6898e9ae8a81d4d4f before, and the identical hash after. That is not "the tests pass again", it is a cryptographic statement that the content is the same content.

The commit hash is new, and that matters. Nothing was rewritten, no history was force-pushed away. The broken state stays in the log where you can go and read what the agent did.

For an autonomous system that is the right shape. You want to undo the damage and keep the evidence, because the failed attempt is your training signal for what to stop the agent doing next time.

Sandbox snapshots and versioned code get talked about as if they solve the same problem. They do not, and picking the wrong one is expensive in both directions.

I ran the same accident on the sandbox side: booted a machine, wrote the code, dropped an 8 MB model artifact next to it, checkpointed, then broke the code and deleted the artifact.

The snapshot brought back the 8 MB artifact. The git rollback would not have, because it was never pushed. That is the whole difference in one file.

A snapshot restores the machine: everything on disk, tracked or not, and it hands you a new sandbox id. Versioned code restores the tree you chose to record, needs no machine to exist, and hands you a new commit on a history you can read.

The part worth pausing on: the entire rollback sequence ran with no sandbox alive.

That is not a detail, it is the operational point. Agent runs are ephemeral. The sandbox that made the mess is usually gone by the time a human notices, torn down at the end of the run or timed out. If your only undo is a snapshot of that machine, your recovery story depends on having predicted the failure well enough to checkpoint before it happened.

Code history does not expire with the run. You can roll back an agent’s work an hour later, from a laptop, with nothing running, and materialise the good tree into a fresh sandbox whenever you next need one.

Rolling back the code was also the fastest of the three operations, at 1028 ms against 1390 ms to take a checkpoint and 2018 ms to restore one.

None of this helps if a human has to notice the breakage. And the stronger move is not to roll main back at all: give each agent a private workspace, and let nothing reach main until it has passed.

I ran two agents against the same base, one of them the broken refactor from earlier:

The broken refactor never reaches main. It still exists, in its own workspace, as a commit you can read and diff, which is what you want when you are trying to work out why an agent keeps failing a task. But main only ever moves to a tree something mechanical has approved.

Three properties make this safe rather than merely tidy.

The workspace is a repository fork, not a sandbox fork, which is the distinction this whole piece turns on. It copies refs rather than a filesystem, and cost 161 and 183 ms in these runs, cheap enough to do per task. The agent starts from the exact base commit and its mistakes are contained by construction rather than by discipline.

If the machine matters as much as the code, take a sandbox checkpoint at the same moment you push the workspace. Both halves of the state then sit behind the same gate, and you still promote only what passed.

expect_oid is a compare-and-swap on the branch you are pushing to. In this loop that is the workspace’s own main, which is the right scope for it: the workspace belongs to one agent, so the guard is there to stop two writers racing on a single branch.

The shared base is looked after one layer up, at promote time, and it holds. I let one agent promote while another was still working, then promoted the second. The merge simply stopped being a fast-forward and became a real three-way merge against the original base, and it came back clean. materialize re-resolves main when it runs rather than trusting the earlier preflight, so a promote that queues behind another one lands on top of it rather than over it. Two guarantees at two layers, each scoped to the job it is doing.

The promotion is gated on a deep preflight. preflight=True computes the merge and writes nothing, and deep=True makes it do the real line-level merge rather than a tree comparison, which is the difference between a correct answer and a conservative guess. That check cost 179 ms.

The gate does not have to be a test suite. A type check, a lint pass, a smoke request, a diff size threshold: anything returning a boolean works. The point is that the agent’s work is provisional until something mechanical says otherwise.

So when do you still need the byte-exact rollback from earlier? For what already landed. An agent promoted before you had this gate, a human pushed directly, a change passed its tests and broke something they did not cover. Isolation prevents; rollback repairs. You want both, and they are the same primitive pointed at different moments.

This is not an argument that snapshots are worse. They answer a question git cannot: what did this machine look like, including the things nobody committed.

Reach for the snapshot when the machine is the state. A long dependency install you do not want to repeat, a GPU environment that took real effort to get right, a heisenbug you want frozen exactly as it occurred.

Reach for versioned code when the code is the state, which for a coding agent is nearly always. It is cheaper, it outlives the sandbox, and it gives you a line-by-line diff of exactly what changed.

Snapshots are simply a different shape from routine code changes, and it is worth being deliberate about which you reach for. A filesystem image is stored whole, compared as a whole, and exists for the moments you chose to capture. That is exactly what you want for an environment, and more than you need for a source tree you are changing many times an hour.

Pass expect_oid on every write. Each push above pins the commit it expects to replace, so a rollback lands on the state you actually looked at rather than one that moved while you were deciding. It is one argument, it costs nothing, and it turns a race into a clean error you can retry.

Rollback is only as good as what you pushed. Untracked build output, caches and model files are not in the tree and will not come back. Decide deliberately what belongs in the repository and what belongs in a snapshot.

The operations log is detailed, down to ref transitions, object counts and pack bytes, and it attributes each operation to the credential that made it. So give each agent role its own API key. That log then becomes per-agent provenance: who moved which ref, when, and by how much.

The useful mental model is that a coding agent needs a version control system, not a time machine for computers.

If you are building anything that lets a model write to a real codebase, the recovery path deserves as much design as the prompt. Record the tree before the agent runs, pin every write to the commit you expect, and keep the broken attempt in the history where you can learn from it. Then a bad refactor at 3am is a one second push instead of an incident.

#9772. Audio8-TTS-Realistic-Air: Edge0's 0.6B Multilingual Text-to-Speech Model Explained

Among other things, launching AIModels.fyi ... Find the right AI model for your project - https://aimodels.fyi

Among other things, launching AIModels.fyi ... Find the right AI model for your project - https://aimodels.fyi

Among other things, launching AIModels.fyi ... Find the right AI model for your project - https://aimodels.fyi

Audio8-TTS-Realistic-Air is Edge0’s 0.6B multilingual text-to-speech model for speech generation with or without a reference voice. It supports zero-shot voice cloning from reference audio and its exact transcript, and lists 23 supported languages. Maintained by Edge0.

Generate speech from text in the 23 listed languages, or clone a voice using a clean reference recording and matching transcript. It can also be deployed through an SGLang Omni adapter with an OpenAI-compatible speech API.

Language quality varies. Reported error-rate and speaker-similarity metrics assess intelligibility and similarity, not perceived realism; the supplied evaluation does not directly quantify realism. Runtime checks were performed on an NVIDIA H20 in BF16, but throughput and streaming were not benchmarked. The model uses custom Transformers code, so loading requires trust_remote_code=True; review repository files before enabling it.

Compared with the earlier Preview release, Realistic Air adds 12 supported languages (23 versus 11). On the reported Seed-TTS aggregate, its error rate is 1.25% versus Preview’s 1.23%, while SIM is 0.704 versus 0.682; the releases were evaluated separately. On the shared eight-language CV3 subset, Realistic Air reports 4.56% error versus Preview’s 4.80%. The supplied reference comparison cautions that different evaluation pipelines and text normalization prevent a strictly matched ranking. Other Audio8 versions include Audio8-TTS-Realistic-0.6b, Audio8-TTS-Preview-0.6b, and Audio8-TTS-Preview-0.1b; the supplied evidence does not establish detailed capability differences for those alternatives.

DualAR architecture: a slow autoregressive transformer predicts one semantic token per audio frame; a fast autoregressive transformer predicts codec codebooks conditioned on the slow hidden state and preceding codebooks. Main model: 601,159,424 parameters, excluding the separately bundled codec. Slow AR: 24 layers, width 896, 14 attention heads, 2 KV heads. Fast AR: 4 layers, width 896, 14 attention heads, 2 KV heads. Audio uses 10 codebooks with 4,096 entries each. The codec operates at 44.1 kHz and 2,048 samples per model frame (about 21.5 frames/s); context is up to 2,048 packed text/audio positions. The repository includes the checkpoint, codec, tokenizer, processor, and custom Transformers code. Python 3.10 or newer and a CUDA-capable GPU are recommended. Runtime smoke tests used PyTorch 2.8.0, Transformers 4.57.3, and an NVIDIA H20 with BF16. License metadata specifies Apache-2.0.

Text is passed to the processor as a list. For voice cloning, provide reference audio and a transcript that exactly matches the spoken content; a clean recording is recommended. Reference-free generation needs only text. The example uses max_new_tokens, temperature, top_p, top_k, and do_sample as generation controls. Supported languages: Cantonese, Chinese, Dutch, English, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Polish, Spanish, Arabic, Finnish, Hindi, Indonesian, Malay, Norwegian, Portuguese, Russian, Swedish, Thai, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

Generation returns audio codes that are decoded by the bundled codec into waveforms. The example writes a WAV file at model.config.codec_sample_rate. The SGLang Omni adapter supports a non-streaming OpenAI-compatible /v1/audio/speech API, reference-free generation, and zero-shot voice cloning.

Q: Can it generate speech without a reference recording?

A: Yes. Pass text to the processor without reference-audio or reference-transcript fields, then use the same generation and decoding steps.

Q: What is required for zero-shot voice cloning?

A: Provide a clean reference recording and a transcript that exactly matches what is spoken in it.

A: The model lists 23 supported languages, including 12 additions over the earlier Preview release.

Q: Does the 0.6B parameter count include the codec?

A: No. The 601,159,424-parameter count is for the main model; the bundled codec is separate.

Q: What software and hardware are recommended?

A: Python 3.10 or newer and a CUDA-capable GPU are recommended. The documented smoke test used PyTorch 2.8.0, Transformers 4.57.3, and BF16 on an NVIDIA H20.

Q: Does the evaluation prove improved perceived realism?

A: No. The reported error-rate and speaker-similarity metrics measure intelligibility and similarity, not perceived realism directly.

A: No. The SGLang Omni runtime check covered a non-streaming speech API; throughput and streaming were not benchmarked.

#9770. Evaluating Large Language Models Beyond Their Demo: A Developer's Guide

When evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs), it's easy to get caught up in their impressive demos. However, to truly understand their strengths and weaknesses, you need to look beyond the surface. This article aims to provide a practical approach to evaluating LLMs effectively. We'll cover the basics, common pitfalls, and a concrete example to help you make informed decisions.

Before diving in, let's establish some context. An LLM is a model trained on vast amounts of text data, allowing it to generate human-like responses to a wide range of inputs. They are incredibly versatile and can be used for various applications, from chatbots to content generation. To evaluate an LLM, you need to consider several factors, not just the demo.

While demos often showcase impressive results, it's important to understand what metrics are being used and how they're calculated. For example, the generation quality is often judged by metrics like BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy) or ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation). Understanding these metrics can help you assess the true quality of the model's outputs.

The performance of an LLM can vary significantly depending on the use case. Consider how well the LLM handles specific tasks such as answering questions, summarizing text, or translating languages. It's crucial to test it on a variety of inputs to get a comprehensive understanding of its capabilities. For instance, you might want to evaluate how well it performs on a dataset of news articles versus a dataset of academic papers.

3. ** **Model Complexity and Training Details

LLM performance can also depend on the complexity of the model and its training details. The size of the model, the type of pre-training, and hyperparameters all play a role. A larger model may perform better, but it also requires more computational resources. Understanding these details can help you evaluate the model's scalability and suitability for your needs.

Concrete Example: Evaluating a Qwen-Style LLM

To illustrate the evaluation process, let's consider a hypothetical LLM called Qwen, which is similar to Alibaba Cloud's Qwen. To evaluate Qwen, you might start by testing it on a dataset of common questions and answers. You can measure the accuracy of the responses and compare them against ground truth. Additionally, you could test Qwen on more complex tasks like summarizing news articles or translating text between different languages. This will help you understand its strengths and weaknesses.

Overlooking Use Case Specificity: Just because an LLM performs well on a demo task, it doesn't mean it will perform equally well in real-world scenarios. Always consider the context and the specific use case before making assumptions.

Focusing Solely on Generation Quality: Generation quality is important, but it's not the only metric you should consider. Other factors like coherence, fluency, and relevance are also crucial. Look at multiple metrics to get a more holistic view of the model.

Ignoring Training Details: The performance of an LLM can vary significantly based on its training details. Don't rely solely on the demo results. Investigate the model's architecture, hyperparameters, and pre-training details to make informed decisions.

Evaluating an LLM goes beyond just looking at their demos. To make the most of their potential, you need to consider a range of factors, including performance metrics, use cases, and training details. By doing so, you can better understand the strengths and weaknesses of the model and choose the most suitable one for your needs. As LLM technology continues to evolve, staying informed and vigilant is key to making the right decisions.

In this article, we explore the top 10 AI tools that are driving innovation and efficiency in various industries. These tools are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The tools included in our list are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for a variety of applications. Some of the tools focus on natural language processing, such as ChatGPT and Grammarly, while others focus on image and video generation, such as DALL-E and Lumen5. #9768. A One-Line JavaScript Bug Broke My GA4 Tracking for Five Months

Frontend developer and founder of BatchSet (batchset.com), a browser-based bulk image converter where files never leave your device. I write about i

Frontend developer and founder of BatchSet (batchset.com), a browser-based bulk image converter where files never leave your device. I write about i

Frontend developer and founder of BatchSet (batchset.com), a browser-based bulk image converter where files never leave your device. I write about i

For five months, Google Analytics told me nobody on my site ever signed up, converted a file, or bought anything. Page views looked fine. Sessions looked fine. The key events report said zero, every day, and I read that as "the funnel is bad" instead of "the funnel is not being recorded".

The bug was one line. This is what it was, why nothing warned me, and how to check your own site in about a minute.

I run BatchSet, a set of browser-based image tools. GA4 is loaded the standard way, with the snippet Google gives you:

Custom events came from a small typed helper in the app code, so components could call trackEvent({ action: "sign_up" }) instead of touching window directly:

It looks like a faithful TypeScript port of the snippet. It is not.

Google's gtag() pushes arguments. Mine pushed args.

arguments is an array-like object. Its type is [object Arguments]. ...args is a rest parameter, and that gives you a real Array. They hold the same values in the same order, and in DevTools they look almost identical:

gtag.js does not treat those two the same. I tested it on the live site: pushing an array sent no hit at all, and pushing an Arguments object with the same three values sent the event. No console error, no warning, no failed request. The array just sat in dataLayer and was never acted on.

I can't point you to a line in Google's docs that says "arrays are ignored". I can tell you what happened on a real production site, and that the fix changed the result.

Page views kept working. The config call comes from Google's own snippet, which uses arguments. So page_view, session_start, first_visit, scroll and user_engagement all arrived. The dashboard looked alive. Only the events from my own helper were missing.

dataLayer looked full. If you open the console and type dataLayer, you see your events sitting there with the right names and parameters. That feels like proof. It only proves the push happened, not that anything read it.

Modern style pushes you toward the bug. Rest parameters are the idiomatic way to write variadic functions now. ESLint even has a core rule, prefer-rest-params, that flags use of arguments. Writing the "clean" version is exactly what breaks it.

On top of that, zero is a believable number for a small site. I had a funnel I had designed and instrumented, and when it read zero I started theorising about why people were leaving, not about whether the instrument worked. That cost more time than the bug itself.

The ..._args parameter is only there so TypeScript accepts calls with arguments. The value that gets pushed is arguments. If you use prefer-rest-params, turn it off for that line and leave a comment, or the next tidy-up will put the bug back.

The simpler option is to not write your own wrapper at all and call window.gtag(...), which is Google's function. I kept the wrapper because it also does a server-side usage record and a consent check, but if yours does nothing extra, delete it.

I also added a test, because this is the kind of thing a refactor reintroduces without anyone noticing:

1. Open your site, open DevTools, and trigger something that should send a custom event.

Google's own entries will say [object Arguments]. If your custom events say [object Array], you have this bug.

3. To be sure, open the Network tab, filter on collect, and trigger the event again. A GA4 hit is a request to .../g/collect with your event name in the en= parameter. No request, no event.

4. In GA4, check Realtime or DebugView, not the standard Events report. The standard reports lag by up to a day, and on the day I deployed the fix they showed zero for everything, including page views. That is processing delay, not a second bug.

After the fix, events started arriving within minutes. Then I hit a quieter problem.

My most visited tool page showed a 2.5% key-event rate. The bulk converter, on similar traffic, showed 28.5%. That looks like a broken page. It wasn't. The resizer's completion event, resize_completed, was firing fine. It just had never been marked as a key event in GA4 Admin, so no report that counts key events included it. Three other tools had the same gap.

Once both problems were fixed, the data finally answered the question I had been guessing at. Over 28 days, on the two biggest tool pages:

Of the people who added a file, 93 to 96% finished the job. The tools work. The loss is one step earlier: roughly four out of five visitors leave without adding anything. I had spent months assuming the conversion flow was the problem, and the flow was the one part that was fine.

These are small numbers from a small site, and I'm not claiming more than they show. But the point stands at any size: check that the instrument records before you trust what it says. A funnel that reads zero is far more often broken tracking than broken product.

That last one is still on my own to-do list.

Frontend developer and founder of BatchSet (batchset.com), a browser-based bulk image converter where files never leave your device. I write about i

#9765. How I think engineers grow when AI writes the first draft

Posted on Nov 4 • Originally published at robertstowe.com

For most of my career an engineer learned the craft by doing the small things first. Fix the typo in the error message, then the off-by-one, then the feature behind a flag, and somewhere in the second year the design of a whole module. AI coding tools now write a decent first draft of most of those small things, and I think that quietly removes the ladder a lot of us climbed.

I do not think the answer is to keep people away from the tools. It is to be deliberate about where the learning now happens.

The typo fix was never about the typo. It taught how the code is organized, how a change gets reviewed, what the tests look like, and how it feels to ship. When a tool does the typing, the person still needs those lessons, and they are no longer free. A manager who wants a junior engineer to learn the codebase has to arrange it on purpose, with a walk through the system, a review that explains instead of approves, and a first change small enough to understand completely.

What the tools do not supply is judgment, such as knowing that the generated code is correct for the wrong reading of the ticket, that it duplicates something two folders away, or that it will be slow at real data volumes. I think judgment grows from reading more code than you write, and from being wrong in public and finding out why. So the growth path I would design now has more reading, more review, and more explaining to others, and less emphasis on lines produced.

Some people say juniors should simply learn the way everyone will work from now on, directing the tools, and that the old ladder is nostalgia. There is something to it. But directing a tool well requires knowing what good looks like, and I have not seen a way to know that without having built things by hand at least a few times. I would keep some work tool-free early on, the way a pilot still learns to fly without the autopilot.

I do not know yet how long the by-hand period should be, or whether it is a period at all rather than a proportion. I also do not know whether the people who start now will end up with a different kind of judgment that is as good as the old kind. Hiring conversations I hear now weigh autonomy and judgment above domain knowledge, and I think that is the right instinct even if nobody can measure it yet.

What I am sure of is that the ladder does not rebuild itself. If a team wants seniors in five years, someone has to decide how juniors learn now.

Photo source: https://photos.robertstowe.com/bengaluru

#9761. What 108 Gumroad Bestsellers Taught Me About Pricing My First 9 Digital Products

Before pricing my first digital products, I did what I always do when I don't know something: I collected data instead of opinions.

I pulled the bestseller rankings for 14 keywords across the Gumroad marketplace â 108 products, live prices, rating counts. Rating count matters because it's the only public proxy for actual sales volume.

Here's what the data showed, and how it shaped the 9 products I launched on Nov 1.

Notion templates cluster in a three-tier ladder: $18 entry, $79 mid, $149 pro. Nobody wins with a single price â the ladder IS the pricing strategy.

Info books / playbooks sell at $20-90. Under $10 reads as "thin content" in this category.

Design assets run $36-99. Higher than most beginners guess.

The most consistent signal in the data: top products in crowded categories price UNDER the category median. Not because their content is worth less â because they're farming reviews first.

Reviews are Gumroad's discovery currency. The algorithm surfaces them, buyers filter by them. A 0-rating $29 product is invisible; a 50-rating $12 product gets discovered and can raise prices later.

Titles of bestsellers almost always promise ONE concrete outcome: a 30-day plan, a specific workflow, a named result. The "Ultimate Guide to X" pattern underperforms everywhere in the data.

In 2 of my 14 categories, the top-ranked products cost $0. You cannot build a business competing with free. Knowing which categories to avoid is arguably more valuable than knowing where to play.

My launch prices, all below category medians:

Day 3 result: 0 sales. I'm publishing that number anyway, because the honest version of "building in public" includes the zeros.

For a small team, it's a good setup. There's no server to babysit, the logs and secrets live in one place, and anyone on the team can read the run history.

It's also a scheduler with fine print, and nearly all of the fine print is about the morning the report doesn't arrive. Here's what GitHub's documentation says about scheduled workflows, what it means for a daily report, and the safeguards that make up for it.

These are all in GitHub's docs for the schedule event, roughly in order of how likely they are to bite.

Scheduled runs can be late, and some never happen. GitHub warns that scheduled runs can be delayed when Actions is under heavy load, that the start of every hour is one of those times, and that under enough load "some queued jobs may be dropped." A dropped run doesn't fail. It just doesn't happen.

Schedules run in UTC unless you say otherwise. Schedules now accept a timezone with an IANA name like America/New_York. Without it, a 7 AM report drifts to 6 AM or 8 AM local twice a year when daylight saving time changes. With it, a time that doesn't exist on the spring-forward day moves to the next valid time.

Schedules only run from the default branch, on its latest commit. Editing a workflow on a feature branch won't tell you whether its schedule works.

In public repositories, schedules switch off after 60 days with no repository activity. A report that just works for two months and then stops is the most frustrating version of all of this.

The shortest interval is five minutes. Irrelevant for a daily report, worth knowing before you build a poller on it.

Most of those lines answer the fine print. The cron is 17 7, not 0 7, because the top of the hour is the busiest time, and a report at 7:17 that arrives beats one at 7:00 that doesn't. workflow_dispatch adds a "Run workflow" button for the mornings the schedule doesn't fire. concurrency stops a manual run and a late scheduled run from overlapping. And the QA rules run as tests before the report does, so a change to the rules can't quietly switch them off.

A daily report should never post a number it can't defend. Before anything goes to the channel, run checks like these:

When a check fails, the report goes to its owner instead of the channel:

Each rule has its own unit test. A held report is a good outcome. It means the bot caught something before a room full of people did.

Retries and manual reruns are good for reliability and bad for a Slack channel. Before posting, check whether today's report is already there:

The marker is the report's own title. A rerun after a successful post does nothing, and a rerun after a held report posts normally once the data is fixed.

None of those checks help when the run never starts. A dropped schedule doesn't fail, so nothing alerts. The answer is a second workflow that runs later and asks one question: did today's report succeed?

It isn't perfect. The watchdog runs on the same scheduler with the same fine print, so it's a second chance, not a guarantee. For a report that really matters, have the bot ping an external heartbeat monitor when it succeeds, and let that service complain when the ping doesn't come. The principle is the same either way: alert on the absence of success, not the presence of failure.

When a report has to arrive at a specific minute, or runs often enough that a few dropped runs a month would matter, use a scheduler that makes promises: a cloud scheduler, Airflow, or a plain cron server you monitor. For one report a day that can arrive at 7:17 or 7:24 without anyone noticing, GitHub Actions is hard to beat. Just read the fine print, and build for the morning it doesn't show up.

#9756. WriteFreely: 49 title matches and an administrator who may be the first user

WriteFreely is a federated publishing platform with a small public footprint in this measurement. On 2026-11-04, ZoomEye returned 49 matches for title="WriteFreely" and zero for app="WriteFreely" with page 1, page size 1 and sub_type=all. A small count does not remove the need to review ownership. A publishing instance can contain unpublished drafts, API tokens and account recovery state.

WriteFreely documentation notes that in some setups the first user to log in becomes the administrator. That behavior can be appropriate for a private instance, but it is dangerous when an installation is exposed before the administrator has been claimed. The setup process must happen inside a controlled network window, with the intended administrator identity established before public discovery.

Inventory the public blog, login path, API endpoint and admin configuration. Check whether federation is enabled and whether instance registration is open. Confirm that the admin claim state is intentional and that a second administrator path cannot be created by an anonymous visitor.

WriteFreely's API documentation describes authentication for actions that create or manage content, while some read operations are public. An API token can represent a publishing account and may have a different blast radius from the server administrator. Record which API tokens exist, what they can do and when they were last used.

Do not place an API token in a public theme, client-side script or repository. Rotate it after a contributor leaves. Check that the token endpoint is protected and that logs do not contain the authorization header.

The absence of an application fingerprint means title matches should not be collapsed into a product count. For owned assets, the title is enough to find the host and compare it with inventory. For external assets, collect only public response metadata.

The 49-title population is manageable, but it is not a vulnerability list. Each result needs a reason to investigate and a boundary that stops before account enumeration or content access.

The 49 matches are a bounded discovery set. The zero application result is a warning that product-specific search will not provide full coverage. An operator can use the title set to compare external visibility with an inventory of owned domains, then verify the highest-risk installations through their own administrator console.

WriteFreely's exposure is often a combination of a public reading surface and a private publishing authority. The security decision is whether those two surfaces are deliberately separated.

#9754. The best apples for apple pie: Here's how to choose.: We put six varieties to the test.

Which are the best pie apples? With apple-picking season hard upon us, it's time to dust off your favorite apple pie recipe, sharpen your crust-rolling skills, and get ready to enjoy fall's favorite dessert: apple pie.

You may be tempted to make your pie from one of the six apple varieties that dominate the domestic market year-round: Red Delicious, Golden Delicious, Gala, Fuji, Granny Smith, and McIntosh.

But when fall rolls around, farmers' markets and orchard farm stands offer an abundance of apple choices.

You've probably identified your favorite eating apple. But what about the best pie apples? They're not necessarily the same. Red and Golden Delicious, for instance, are reliably crisp, sweet-eating apples. But when you bake them into a pie, they can become mushy and lose some of their sweetness. So what are the best apples for pie?

We'll put six different pie apples to the test.

The pie apples: I decide to put two of my favorites, Golden Russet and Northern Spy, up against a couple of classic pie apples: McIntosh and Cortland. I also add Granny Smith because, if there's one ubiquitous, year-round apple, Granny Smith is it. Ginger Gold — a Golden Delicious cross with Albemarle Pippin — is another variety that's often available in fall, and a worthy representative of the Delicious family.

And yes, there are plenty of other apple varieties to choose from: Fuji, Gala, Honey Crisp, and so many more. But with limited time and resources — and a pan with space for just six pies — I'm not able to test every apple out there. But if you want to choose the best pie apples among your personal favorites, you can have fun doing this same test at home.

I use a muffin tin to bake apples sweetened with a bit of sugar. To mimic apple pie (sans crust), I pile sliced apples high in the pan. Then I bake them in a preheated 425°F oven for 20 minutes, lower the oven temperature to 375°F, and continue to bake the apples until they're bubbly, about 40 minutes.

I had no idea there'd be such significant differences in both texture and flavor. For example, Russets and Macs are sweetened with the same amount of sugar, bake at the same temperature, for the same amount of time —  and offer way different results.

So, Granny Smith looks like the best combination of both taste and texture. Does it make the very best apple pie?

Not necessarily. I've baked many pies with this all-purpose apple, especially during the winter when other apples are scarce or pricey. A pie made 100% with Granny Smith apples is a mighty fine pie. But in fall, when every apple variety in the world is seemingly at your fingertips, why not take advantage of one or two (or more) of your own local favorites?

At the end of the day, choosing the best pie apples is a personal decision. My best apple pie would include a combination of these three: Cortland, for flavor; Russet, for texture; and Granny Smith, for its combination of the two.

What apples would fill your best pie? Bake your favorite varieties side by side and see what happens; the results may surprise you.

Please share your favorite apples for pie — and your favorite apple pie tips! — in comments, below.

#9750. How to prebake pie crust — and why you should: The key to flaky — not flabby — pie crust.

A soggy bottom. Not something you want for your baby. Or your pie crust. And while we can’t help you with your baby, there’s a simple solution to pies with soggy bottoms: prebake (also known as blind bake) the crust.

There are a number of reasons your pie can end up with a soft, pale, underbaked crust — and steps you can take to help prevent that unfortunate result.

But the one surefire way to make certain your pie’s crust will be golden brown, crisp, and delicious — just as appealing as its filling — is to prebake it. That’s right: bake the bottom crust first, before adding the filling.

Most commonly, it's smart to prebake pie crust when:

But some fillings might instead cook fully on the stovetop, like the rich, thick filling for chocolate cream pie. When it’s done, you simply pour it into its crust — and said crust had better be prebaked to perfection, since the pie’s not going anywhere near an oven.

Other pies, typically those with a more delicate, egg- and cream-based filling (think custard pie or quiche) require at least some baking — but don’t spend long enough in the oven (at a high enough temperature) to guarantee a fully baked, brown and crispy crust.

In these cases, you need to prebake your crust.

The recipe you're following may explain explicitly how to prebake your crust. But if it doesn't, follow this process:

First, roll your bottom crust and place it in the pan. Crimp or flatten the edge. Chill it for 30 minutes, to relax the gluten and firm up the fat(s); this will help prevent shrinkage, so don't skip!

Line the crust with foil, parchment, or a paper coffee filter. Fill it about two-thirds full with dried beans, uncooked rice (or other uncooked grain berries), pie weights, or granulated sugar.

Bake the crust in a preheated 375°F oven for 20 minutes, set on a baking stone or steel if you have one. Remove the crust from the oven and lift out the liner and weights. (If you’ve used sugar, save it for your future baking; it’ll be lightly toasted and yummy!)

At this point your crust is partially prebaked, and good for any of your pies that tend to exhibit a wan, flabby bottom crust when done. Think pumpkin pie: You don’t want to bake the filling so long that it’s stiff and dry, but you may pull your pie out of the oven to find your perfectly baked filling is resting in a partially baked crust. Prebaking your crust partway is a sensible solution for this scenario.

To fully prebake the crust, prick the bottom all over with a fork to prevent bubbles. Return the crust to the oven and bake for an additional 20 to 25 minutes, until it’s golden all over.

If, despite your best efforts, the lined, weighted crust still slips down the inside of the pan while it prebakes, try this: Bake the crust upside down.

To start, you’ll need two identical (or nicely nestable) pie pans with flat rims.

Place your rolled-out crust in one of the pans, anchoring it to the rim of the pan with a fork-tine crimp. Place a liner of some kind (same as above: parchment, foil, coffee filter) into the pan. Nest the second pan into the first.

Pick up both pans, turn them over, and set them on a baking sheet. Place the baking sheet and pie pans in the oven, and bake as directed above. As the crust bakes, gravity will pull it down toward its rim — rather than into a puddle at the bottom of the pan. Magic!

After 20 minutes remove the baking sheet from the oven, carefully turn the pans over, lift out the empty pan, and remove the liner. At this point, your crust is partially prebaked. To prebake it fully, place the crust back in the oven, right side up, and bake until it's golden.

If you struggle with a pale, pasty bottom crust in your fruit pie, then yes, you can prebake it — with a couple of caveats:

So, soggy bottoms begone! From now on I expect every pie you bake will have a deep golden brown, flaky, crispy crust on the bottom — all because of the prebake.

And if you have any other questions about pie — from creating tender, flaky crust to thickening fruit filling to assessing when your pie is perfectly baked — please check out our Pie Baking Guide.

Perfect For: Marketing teams, copywriters, and businesses needing high-converting marketing copy across multiple channels.

The AI tools listed here are revolutionizing the content creation landscape in 2025, making it easier than ever to produce high-quality, engaging, and impactful content. By integrating these tools into your workflow, you can save time, unleash your creativity, and achieve better results.

#9747. Does opting out of TV tracking work?

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

A new study from Northeastern University shows that while most TV operating systems respect ACR opt-outs, not all do.﻿

A new study from Northeastern University shows that while most TV operating systems respect ACR opt-outs, not all do.﻿

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The fact our TVs are gathering our information isn’t new, but what and how they’re tracking — and if we can stop it — is hard to figure out. Researchers at Northeastern University monitored 12 TVs from 10 manufacturers to test whether opting out of automatic content recognition (ACR) actually works. While opting out was effective for most TVs — including LG, Amazon Fire TV, a Sony Bravia running Google TV, and those with Vidaa OS (which can be found on TVs from Hisense, Toshiba, and smaller brands like the Supersonic used in the study) — Samsung and Roku kept sending some data. And Walmart’s Vizio TV continued on as if the opt-out hadn’t even happened.

ACR systems sample the audio or video playing on a TV, convert them into digital fingerprints, and send them to a database to identify what’s being watched. TV companies use that information to make recommendations of what to watch next, provide viewing metrics, and allow for targeted ads.

The researchers wanted to understand when ACR was running on each TV, whether opting out did anything, and what type of data ACR systems were capturing. Because there are many different TV operating systems, and manufacturers keep smart TVs locked down, ACR activity needs to be inferred based on where the TV sends data.

Hisense 32A4K (with no ACR) — Google TV OS

Sony KD32W830K (with no ACR) — Google TV OS

To answer those questions, the team developed a suite of automated experiments across all the TV operating systems. They used Northeastern’s Mon(IoT)r software and SPHERE Research Infrastructure testbeds to capture and analyze all network traffic from each TV, which let them determine when ACR tracking was active and figure out where the TVs were likely sending that data.

They played content on each TV from first-party streaming services such as LG Channels and The Roku Channel; third-party streaming like Netflix and YouTube; over an HDMI cable; using the over-the-air antenna; and via screen mirroring, all to see if there was any difference in ACR traffic on different inputs.

They found that several of the TVs tested didn’t seem to have any ACR activity whatsoever, including a Westinghouse Xumo TV and three TVs from Sony, Hisense, and TCL running Google TV OS. (Another Sony TV with Google TV did have ACR enabled.)

Of the TVs with ACR-associated network traffic, all of them scan over-the-air transmissions, while everyone but Google and Amazon uses it on first-party streaming services (such as The Roku Channel and LG Channels).

Third-party apps like Netflix and YouTube? No ACR except a small amount on webOS, which disappears when opted out. Screen mirroring also looks to be safe from monitoring on all TVs but the one running Vidaa OS.

To figure out whether each OS used audio or video fingerprinting, the experimenters played content that had both video and audio, just audio with a black screen, and just video with no audio, and watched for changes in network traffic to the ACR endpoints. They found that Tizen likely uses video fingerprinting, webOS and Vidaa use audio, and Fire TV OS, Google TV OS, Roku OS, and Vizio OS use a combination of both.

Ideally, opting out of ACR activity should stop all data transmission to suspected ACR endpoints, and for webOS, Fire OS, Vidaa OS, and the Sony Google TV, that’s what happened. But it wasn’t always the case. Samsung’s Tizen OS activity decreased, but not completely, with ACR-correlated traffic still showing while using the antenna, first-party streaming, and HDMI. And on the two Roku OS TVs (one from TCL and one from Roku), ACR still applied to the Roku Channel app. TCL discloses this limitation in menu settings, while the Roku TV does not. Opting out on the Vizio TV didn’t change ACR-correlated traffic at all. (Vizio settled a lawsuit with the FTC in 2017 related to consumer data gathering.) I reached out to Walmart for comment about the Vizio TV’s performance in the study but did not hear back before press time.

As the paper notes, because almost all network traffic sent from the TVs to the suspected ACR endpoints was encrypted, the researchers couldn’t be entirely sure that the traffic that remained after opting out was ACR traffic.

“We interpret the continued presence of traffic consistent with ACR tracking after opt-out as suspicious, though we cannot confirm the contents of the network traffic (due to encryption), nor whether data is processed or retained on the server side.”

It doesn’t seem to matter if you opt out during the setup process or later down the line. “For the large-scale automated tests, we applied the opt-out through the TVs’ settings menus after setup, not during the setup process,” project lead professor David Choffnes told The Verge via email. But the researchers “also manually tested certain TVs (the Vizio TV and the Fire TV) after a factory reset, and the results were unchanged,” he told me. The testing order was also randomized to prevent earlier experiments from influencing later ones.

Disturbingly, during the study, the researchers discovered a vulnerability with Vidaa OS exposing unencrypted information. Because of the vulnerability, the researchers were able to access an MQTT broker — an intermediary between Vidaa OS and Unruly, a video ad platform — and receive ACR results from other Vidaa TV users.

“Each message carries a Client ID, a permanent identifier for the TV that can’t be reset, along with the time zone, the app name, the input (antenna, HDMI), the antenna channel and an audio fingerprint.”

Over a period of three hours, they collected data from over 1 million unique TVs. They informed Vidaa of the vulnerability, which the company confirmed and has since addressed by requiring a login for the server (although messages are still sent unencrypted).

The paper recommends ways to protect ourselves from TVs harvesting our data. The easiest is to disconnect your TV from the internet, both wired and wireless, and instead use a streaming device that doesn’t run ACR.

If you want to continue using the built-in apps, they suggest using webOS, Fire TV OS, Google TV on Sony, and Vidaa OS — just make sure to opt out of everything you can. They also provide a blocklist of endpoints you can restrict using blockers like Pi-hole that don’t break the TVs or affect view quality.

I agree that there needs to be more transparency from TV manufacturers about ACR and, more broadly, what data of ours they collect and when. The Northeastern study helps to pinpoint when data is gathered, but there’s still a lot that’s seemingly intentionally hidden. And it shouldn’t be up to independent researchers to discover and disclose any of this. It should be the responsibility of the companies doing the collecting. It’s time for them to stop hiding what they’re doing.
